title: Moggallana's powers
hookLine: foremost in psychic power, and still humble

cards: On the path down from Vulture Peak, the hill outside Rajagaha, Moggallana smiles. His companion on the walk, Lakkhana, notices and asks what any friend would ask: why the smile?
And Moggallana, who in the texts could see things no one around him saw, doesn't answer. Not here, he says. Ask me again when we're with the Buddha.
That small refusal on a dusty path is a good door into a man whose powers were well-known. The texts care about what he could do. They seem to care even more about how he carried it.

teach.b: First, the reputation. In the Anguttara Nikaya's list of foremost disciples, the Buddha names Moggallana foremost in psychic power.
Earlier on this path we watched him, in another discourse, shake a palace of the gods with his toe.

Later, before the Buddha, Lakkhana asks again, and now Moggallana tells it: on the path he saw a suffering being, a body of bones, tormented by birds as it moved through the air. And the Buddha backs him up.

In paraphrase: I saw that being too, once, but I didn't speak of it. Others wouldn't have believed me, and that would have been to their harm. So the power is real in the story, and so is the restraint.
Say it when it can help, and not before. Third, his slips. In a whole chapter of the Samyutta Nikaya, Moggallana tells his fellow monks how his own meditation went.
He reached a deep stillness, and lost it. Distraction crept back in. And the Buddha, he says, came to him and said: Moggallana, don't be careless.

Then the next stage, and the same thing again. He ends, in paraphrase: if anyone is a disciple who reached greatness with the teacher's help, it's me. The strongest one in the room, telling everyone where he kept falling.

teach.h: A MIRROR FOR YOUR OWN FACE.
teach.b: In the Majjhima Nikaya he teaches monks to check themselves the way someone looks in a mirror: seeing a smudge on their face, they wipe it off, and seeing none, they're glad.
Power, in his hands, keeps turning back into honesty about himself.

how: In Theravada communities Moggallana is honored with Sariputta as one of the Buddha's two chief disciples, and in some temples their images stand on either side of the Buddha.

o: the authority to lead the monks after the Buddha
psychic abilities he used with restraint
magic tricks he performed to win followers

p: saw it too, and kept quiet
the Buddha's word when he slipped

s: Moggallana told Lakkhana what he saw right away
he said: ask me again when we're with the Buddha.
Moggallana said he reached his attainments on his own
he called himself a disciple who reached greatness with the teacher's help.
Moggallana taught monks to look at themselves like a face in a mirror
see a smudge, wipe it off; see none, be glad.

games.q: you're Moggallana. on the path you've seen something no one else can see, and your friend asks why you smiled. what do you do?
o: say: ask me again when we're with the Buddha.
laugh it off and never mention it.
games.why: he waits. in front of the Buddha he tells it, and the Buddha says he once saw the same being but kept quiet, because people wouldn't have believed him.

practice: Name one thing you're good at, cooking, spreadsheets, calming a crying child, and let yourself admit it's real.
Then, like Moggallana, recall one time that strength slipped, or someone helped you get it back, and hold both at once, the strength and the help, as you rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Moggallana's powers. Named foremost in psychic power, he holds back what he sees until it can help, tells where he slipped, and teaches the mirror. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: power, success; the word the texts use for Moggallana's psychic powers.

carryVoice: Your line: power, humbly. The strongest one told everyone where he slipped. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 1.189 (Etadagga Vagga: foremost in psychic power)
